To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the cultivation of microaeraerophilic FeII‐oxidizing bacteria can be optimized by the application of gradient tubes with FeS and/or zero‐valent Fe as FeII‐source, by transfer of the cultures to fresh tubes after 2‐3 days and by avoiding FeCO3 and/or FeCl2 as FeII‐sources.
The temporal development of the O2 and Fe(II) gradients in agar‐based gradient cultures was quantitatively monitored for the first time.

the classical approach for the growth of microaerophiles in agar‐based gradient cultures can be improved by the quantification of the temporal development of the O2 and Fe(II) concentration profile over time.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new method to study and cultivate microaerophilically Fe(II) oxidizing bacteria.
the cultivation of microaeriaophic Fe(II)-oxidizers and provides a basis for future studies on the ecology of these organisms in the environment
the development and application of a new approach to study the growth of microaerophiles and the formation and transformation of iron(III) minerals in gradient tubes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
FeS and zerovalent Fe are the most suitable Fe(II) sources for the isolation and cultivation of freshwater and/or marine microaerobic Fe(II) oxidizers.

Fe(III) precipitation and Fe(II) consumption by microbially mediated Fe(II) oxidizers is not the only reason why Fe(II) concentrations in gradient tubes decline with increasing distance from the tube bottom.

gradient tubes are an excellent method to culture microaerophil Fe(II) oxidizers, but that the use of different Fe(III)‐precursors and the transfer of the culture to fresh tubes is crucial for the cultivation of these bacteria.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
gradient tubes provide a simple, yet reliable tool to cultivate microaerophillic Fe(II) oxidizers.
gradient tubes represent a useful tool to cultivate microaerophilically growing Fe(II) oxidizers.
microbially induced Fe(III) mineral precipitation is the key factor for the development of the gradient tubes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cultivation of microaersophilic Fe(III)‐precipitating bacteria can be improved by the use of FeS and zero-valent iron powder, which are more suitable Fe(II) sources than FeCO3 or FeCl2.
microaerophilicity and the use of Fe(II) as energy source are not necessarily linked, but can be uncoupled.
microsensors provide an excellent tool for quantitative monitoring of O2 and dissolved Fe(III) and Fe(II) in gradient tubes.
